newsitem.title: JAMAICA: Former Jamaica prime minister Manley laid to rest.
newsitem.headline: Former Jamaica prime minister Manley laid to rest.

text.p: Thousands of people paid their respects to former Jamaican prime minister Michael Manley on Sunday, filling the main cathedral and spilling into the streets for the funeral of the legendary Caribbean leader.

Manley's flag-draped casket was carried on the shoulders of a military honour guard, preceded by 16 officiating clergymen and followed by leading dignitaries including former Venzuelan president Carlos Andres Perez, Haitian President Rene Preval and Cuban President Fidel Castro.

Castro's arrival earlier was greeted by roars from the crowd and shouts of "Fidel, Fidel," and by a standing ovation from those inside the cathedral. The only other dignitary to get such a welcome was Nation of Islam leader Louis Farrakhan.

Manley, the son of the architect of Jamaica's political independence Norman Manley, died of cancer at his home March 6. He was dubbed "Joshua" in the 1970s, because his father never served as prime minister after independence, thus leaving it to his son to lead Jamaica into the "promised land."

Castro took several minutes to chat with Manley's five children, Preval and with Farrakhan. The Cuban leader was last in Jamaica in 1977 at the height of Cuban-Jamaican cooperation, a fact which further soured Manley's relations with Washington.

The only tense moment occurred at the graveside, when Antigua's prime minister Lester Bird fainted and had to be helped to a waiting ambulance. However he was back on his feet and taking his place among the dignitaries 15 minutes later.

Tributes were read at the service by Jamaica's prime minister, and Manley's successor, P.J. Patterson, and by former prime minister, and Manley's cousin Hugh Shearer, whom Manley defeated in the 1972 elections.

Schoolmate and former cabinet minister David Coore remembered the schoolboy Manley as one who would "champion the cause of those who were bullied or picked on by the bigger boys," a trait that Coore said he carried into his later political life and even onto the international stage.

Patterson recalled Manley as a cricket historian, the last living founder of the Caribbean Community (Caricom), and a leader in the international anti-apartheid struggle, the Commonwealth, and the non-aligned movement.
"Take heart that this world is a much better place because he shared his time and talent with so many," Patterson said.

The funeral and burial were broadcast by virtually all of Jamaica's radio and TV stations, with taped tributes from a number of dignitaries including Farrakhan, Preval, Perez, and former U.S. ambassador to the United Nations Andrew Young.

Preval called him "a man of great wisdom," Andres Perez recalled he was a "major pillar in Socialist International," while Farrakhan stated he was "a great soul among the great prophets and teachers."

Recalling Manley's nickname from the 1970s, Farrakhan said "he did that which was unpopular, but he did what he believed was morally and ethically correct, and that's why the people of Jamaica called him Joshua."

Following the service was a one-hour procession along the one-mile (1.6 km) route from the church to his final resting place. The casket was drawn on a gun carriage with full military honours, followed by Patterson, Castro and the other dignitaries along with thousands of other people.
Manley was buried at National Heroes park in Kingston, alongside his father Norman, his mother Edna, and other leading Jamaican political figures.
